stem: What does the ServiceNow Change Management application provide?

options.text: A systematic approach to control the lifecycle of all changes, enabling beneficial changes with minimum disruption to IT services
A way to restore service as fast as possible after an outage
A method to find the root cause of recurring incidents
A catalog for ordering hardware and software

rationale: Change Management is the controlled on-ramp for modifying services: a systematic lifecycle that lets useful changes happen while keeping disruption to a minimum.

distractor_notes.B: Restoring service fast is Incident Management.
distractor_notes.C: Root cause hunting is Problem Management.
distractor_notes.D: Ordering items is Request Management / Service Catalog.

stem: Which three types of service change does ServiceNow Change Management support, per ITIL?

options.text: Standard, emergency, and normal
Major, minor, and cosmetic
Pre-approved, post-approved, and rejected
Incident, problem, and request

rationale: ServiceNow follows ITIL's three change types: standard, emergency, and normal. Each carries its own process expectations.

distractor_notes.B: Major/minor/cosmetic isn't the ServiceNow change-type set.
distractor_notes.C: Approval status isn't how the types are named.
distractor_notes.D: Incident, problem, and request are separate ITSM processes, not change types.

stem: What does the change type of a change request determine?

options.text: Which state model is invoked and the change process that must be followed
The CMDB class of the affected CI
The caller's notification preferences
The instance's release version

rationale: Choosing the change type isn't cosmetic — it selects the state model and the process the change must travel through, from approvals to scheduling.

distractor_notes.B: The CI's class comes from the CMDB, independent of change type.
distractor_notes.C: Notification preferences are user settings, not driven by change type.
distractor_notes.D: The release version is a platform attribute, unrelated to change type.

stem: Which description best fits a standard change?

options.text: A pre-authorized, low-risk, repeatable change with a proven history of success that follows a specified procedure
A high-priority change that bypasses normal approvals to resolve an outage
Any change that is neither standard nor emergency
A change that always requires CAB authorization

rationale: Standard changes are the routine, proven, low-risk ones — pre-authorized and following a set procedure, so they don't need fresh approvals each time.

distractor_notes.B: That describes an emergency change.
distractor_notes.C: That describes a normal change.
distractor_notes.D: Standard changes are pre-approved and specifically skip CAB authorization.

stem: Because standard changes are pre-approved, which approval steps do they skip?

options.text: Group/peer approval and CAB authorization
The creation of the change record
All implementation tasks
The closure of the change

rationale: Pre-approval is the whole point of a standard change: it streamlines the flow by skipping group/peer approval and CAB authorization, since the change is already vetted.

distractor_notes.B: You still create the change record — it's the approvals that are streamlined.
distractor_notes.C: Implementation tasks still happen; the change still has to be done.
distractor_notes.D: Closure still occurs at the end of the change.

stem: A critical security patch must be deployed immediately to stop an active exploit. Which change type applies, and what is distinctive about its approval path?

options.text: Emergency change — it bypasses group and peer review and goes straight to the Authorize state for the CAB approval group
Standard change — it needs no record because it is pre-approved
Normal change — it must complete two full levels of approval before any action
It is not a change at all; it should be logged only as an incident

rationale: An urgent fix like a security patch is an emergency change. Speed matters, so it skips group and peer review and jumps straight to Authorize for the CAB approval group.

distractor_notes.B: Standard changes are pre-approved but still create a record; an urgent unproven patch isn't a standard change anyway.
distractor_notes.C: Waiting for two full approval levels defeats the urgency of an emergency.
distractor_notes.D: Deploying a patch is a change; the incident may be what triggered it, but the patch itself is a change.

stem: What does a normal change require before it is implemented?

options.text: A prescriptive process with assessments and authorizations, including peer/technical approval and CAB authorization
No approvals at all
Only the caller's confirmation
Immediate implementation that bypasses all review

rationale: Normal changes go the full distance: assessments and multiple authorizations — peer/technical, change management, and CAB — to keep disruption low before they're implemented, reviewed, and closed.

distractor_notes.B: No approvals describes a standard change, which is pre-approved.
distractor_notes.C: Caller confirmation isn't the authorization mechanism for a normal change.
distractor_notes.D: Bypassing review is an emergency-change trait, not normal.

stem: How is a normal change defined relative to the other change types?

options.text: Any service change that is not a standard change or an emergency change
Only changes that resolve major incidents
Only pre-approved catalog-based changes
Changes that never touch configuration items

rationale: Normal is the catch-all: if a change isn't a pre-approved standard change or an urgent emergency change, it's a normal change and follows the full prescriptive process.

distractor_notes.B: Resolving major incidents urgently points to an emergency change.
distractor_notes.C: Pre-approved catalog-based changes are standard changes.
distractor_notes.D: Whether CIs are touched doesn't define the normal type.

stem: What is the purpose of creating a change request?

options.text: To implement a controlled process for modifying approved and supported configuration items
To document an unplanned service outage
To request access to a knowledge base
To record a customer's satisfaction score

rationale: A change request wraps a controlled process around modifying approved, supported CIs — so changes happen deliberately rather than ad hoc.

distractor_notes.B: An unplanned outage is an incident.
distractor_notes.C: Knowledge access isn't what a change request is for.
distractor_notes.D: Satisfaction scores relate to incidents/requests, not change creation.

stem: How are approved standard changes typically made available for efficient, repeatable requesting?

options.text: As a catalog of predefined standard change templates
As individual incidents
As CMDB identification rules
As problem tasks

rationale: Approved standard changes live as templates in a standard change catalog, which makes requesting them quick and lets the Change team control exactly what's authorized as standard.

distractor_notes.B: Incidents track disruptions, not reusable standard changes.
distractor_notes.C: Identification rules are CMDB configuration.
distractor_notes.D: Problem tasks belong to Problem Management.

stem: How does a user raise a new standard change quickly?

options.text: By creating it from a published standard change catalog template
By submitting it for full CAB authorization first
By converting an incident into a change
By editing the CMDB schema

rationale: Standard changes are raised straight from published catalog templates — the template carries the pre-approved details, so the requester just fills in specifics.

distractor_notes.B: Standard changes are pre-approved and don't go to CAB authorization.
distractor_notes.C: Promoting an incident creates a change, but the streamlined standard-change path is the catalog template.
distractor_notes.D: Editing the CMDB schema has nothing to do with raising a standard change.

references.title: Create a standard change request from the catalog

stem: What is the purpose of change templates?

options.text: To standardize the creation of change requests, based on the available change models
To delete change records in bulk
To calculate the CMDB health score
To assign incidents to groups

rationale: Change templates make change creation consistent by basing new requests on defined change models — less re-keying, fewer mistakes, more repeatability.

distractor_notes.B: Templates create standardized changes; they don't bulk-delete records.
distractor_notes.C: CMDB health is a Data Foundations metric.
distractor_notes.D: Incident assignment is handled by incident assignment rules.

stem: What happens to files attached to a standard change template when a change request is created from it?

options.text: The attached files are copied to the change request created from the template
The files are deleted from the template
The files are emailed to the CAB manager
The files are uploaded to the CMDB

rationale: Attachments on a standard change template carry over: the change request created from the template gets a copy of those files, so supporting docs travel with the change.

distractor_notes.B: The template keeps its files; copies go to the new change.
distractor_notes.C: There's no automatic email to the CAB manager.
distractor_notes.D: Attachments aren't pushed into the CMDB.

references.title: Attach files to a standard change template

stem: What is a change task?

options.text: A piece of work related to a change request, such as planning, implementing, testing, and reviewing the change
A pre-approved catalog item
A record that documents the root cause of incidents
A CMDB relationship between two CIs

rationale: Change tasks break a change into the actual work — plan it, implement it, test it, review it — so the steps can be tracked and assigned individually under the parent change.

distractor_notes.B: A catalog item is a request offering, not a change task.
distractor_notes.C: Documenting root cause is a Problem Management activity.
distractor_notes.D: CI relationships live in the CMDB, not as change tasks.

stem: How can you automate routing change requests to the appropriate group or individual?

options.text: Define change request assignment rules
Run conflict detection
Create a known error article
Enable the auto-close property

rationale: Assignment rules automate the routing of change requests to the right group or person, so changes don't sit unassigned waiting for manual triage.

distractor_notes.B: Conflict detection finds scheduling clashes; it doesn't assign work.
distractor_notes.C: Known errors belong to Problem Management.
distractor_notes.D: Auto-close relates to incidents, not change assignment.

references.title: Create a change request assignment rule

stem: What does creating a change request from a configuration item (CI) let you do?

options.text: Create a change from a list of CIs, or add selected CIs from a list to a change record
Delete the CI from the CMDB
Convert the CI into an incident
Reset the CI's discovery source

rationale: Starting from CIs lets you spin up a change directly from a list of them, or attach selected CIs to a change — handy when you already know which items the change will touch.

distractor_notes.B: Creating a change doesn't delete the CI.
distractor_notes.C: CIs aren't converted into incidents.
distractor_notes.D: Discovery source isn't reset by creating a change from a CI.

references.title: Create a change request from a configuration item (CI)

stem: How can additional affected CIs or services be associated with a change request?

options.text: Through related lists on the Change Request form, and from the dependency views map
Only by editing the CMDB schema
Only through a MID Server
Only by the original caller

rationale: You attach affected CIs and services using the related lists on the change form, and you can also pull them in visually from the dependency views map.

distractor_notes.B: You don't need to alter the CMDB schema to associate CIs with a change.
distractor_notes.C: A MID Server is discovery infrastructure, not how you associate CIs on a change.
distractor_notes.D: Any appropriately permitted user can associate CIs, not only the caller.

references.title: Associated CIs on a change request

stem: After creating a change request, what can you do to evaluate it before scheduling?

options.text: Assess and analyze the risk and impact, and review any conflicts that are detected
Automatically promote it to a major incident
Delete all related change tasks
Convert it into a problem

rationale: Before you commit to a window, you assess the change's risk and impact and review any detected conflicts — the homework that keeps a change from causing more harm than good.

distractor_notes.B: Changes aren't promoted to major incidents.
distractor_notes.C: Deleting tasks isn't part of risk/impact analysis.
distractor_notes.D: Converting to a problem is unrelated to assessing change risk.

references.title: Analyze change request risk and impact

stem: What does the risk lookup table use to determine a change's calculated risk value?

options.text: The success probability value and the impact value
The caller's location and language
The number of attached knowledge articles
The CMDB discovery schedule

rationale: The risk lookup table maps the calculated risk from the change's success probability and its impact — combining how likely it is to succeed with how much it would affect if it didn't.

distractor_notes.B: Caller location/language doesn't feed the risk calculation.
distractor_notes.C: Attached articles don't determine risk.
distractor_notes.D: The discovery schedule is unrelated to risk scoring.

stem: What does the change success score help you determine?

options.text: How likely a team is to complete the change request without issues, based on historical data
The number of CIs in the CMDB
The caller's satisfaction with the service desk
Which incidents to auto-close

rationale: The change success score taps a team's historical performance to estimate how likely they are to land the change cleanly — useful signal when weighing risk.

distractor_notes.B: CI counts come from the CMDB, not the success score.
distractor_notes.C: Satisfaction surveys relate to incidents/requests.
distractor_notes.D: Auto-close is an incident behavior, unrelated to change success scoring.

stem: On what basis does conflict detection identify potential scheduling conflicts for a change request?

options.text: The configuration items and the planned start and end dates, also checking blackout/maintenance schedules and other active changes
The caller's time zone only
The number of approvals on the change
The change's category alone

rationale: Conflict detection looks at which CIs are involved and the planned start/end window, then cross-checks blackout and maintenance schedules and other active changes to flag clashes.

distractor_notes.B: Time zone alone doesn't drive conflict detection.
distractor_notes.C: Approval count isn't a conflict input.
distractor_notes.D: Category alone doesn't determine scheduling conflicts.

stem: Which of the following conditions can cause conflict detection to flag a change request?

options.text: The CI is already scheduled at the given date and time
The CI is in a blackout window
The CI is not in its maintenance window
The change is categorized as a standard change
The CI has no associated knowledge articles

rationale: Conflicts fire when a CI (or its parent/child) is already scheduled, sits in a blackout window, or falls outside its maintenance window — all genuine scheduling clashes. Change type and knowledge articles are irrelevant to scheduling conflicts.

distractor_notes.D: Being a standard change is a process attribute, not a scheduling conflict trigger.
distractor_notes.E: Knowledge article counts have nothing to do with scheduling conflicts.

stem: What does the conflict calendar provide, and what tool helps resolve the conflicts it shows?

options.text: A graphical view of potential scheduling conflicts, with the Scheduling Assistant to help resolve them
A list of CMDB identification rules, resolved with the IRE
A record of caller satisfaction, resolved with a survey
A library of knowledge articles, resolved with KCS

rationale: The conflict calendar paints the scheduling conflicts visually — active changes, blackout schedules, and out-of-maintenance windows — and the Scheduling Assistant helps you shuffle the change to a clean slot.

distractor_notes.B: Identification rules and the IRE are CMDB / Data Foundations topics.
distractor_notes.C: Satisfaction surveys aren't what the conflict calendar shows.
distractor_notes.D: Knowledge articles and KCS are Knowledge Management.

stem: You changed a change request's planned start time and want to immediately re-check for clashes before submitting. What can you do?

options.text: Run conflict detection manually for the change request and review the detected conflicts
Delete the maintenance schedule
Promote the change to a major incident
Set the change to On Hold with reason Awaiting Caller

rationale: You don't have to wait for the automatic run — you can trigger conflict detection manually for the change and review whatever conflicts come back, then adjust the schedule.

distractor_notes.B: Deleting the maintenance schedule removes a guardrail rather than checking for clashes.
distractor_notes.C: Changes aren't promoted to major incidents.
distractor_notes.D: Awaiting Caller is an incident On Hold reason, not a change action.

stem: What does a maintenance schedule define?

options.text: The periods during which a configuration item or change can be implemented
The root cause of an incident
The CMDB class hierarchy
The caller's notification channel

rationale: Maintenance schedules mark the windows when it's acceptable to implement a CI or change — work outside those windows is what conflict detection flags.

distractor_notes.B: Root cause is Problem Management.
distractor_notes.C: The CMDB class hierarchy is Data Foundations.
distractor_notes.D: Notification channels are user/notification settings.

stem: A normal change is planned during a defined change blackout window for a critical CI. What is the appropriate way to surface and address this before implementation?

options.text: Conflict detection flags the blackout window, and you reschedule the change to a valid maintenance window
Ignore it, since blackout windows do not apply to normal changes
Convert the change into a standard change to bypass scheduling rules
Delete the CI from the change so no conflict is detected

rationale: Conflict detection catches the blackout overlap; the right move is to reschedule into a valid maintenance window rather than push through a freeze. Normal changes are meant to land outside blackout windows and inside maintenance windows.

distractor_notes.B: Blackout windows absolutely apply to normal changes.
distractor_notes.C: Reclassifying to dodge scheduling rules is gaming the process, not a fix.
distractor_notes.D: Stripping the CI hides the conflict instead of resolving the real scheduling risk.

stem: What view does the Change Schedules module provide of change requests?

options.text: A Gantt or timeline view based on criteria defined in a Change Schedule Definition
A pie chart of incident categories
A CMDB dependency map only
A list of knowledge articles

rationale: The Change Schedules module lays changes out on a Gantt or timeline view, driven by the criteria in a Change Schedule Definition — so you can see what's planned and when at a glance.

distractor_notes.B: Incident category charts aren't what the change schedule shows.
distractor_notes.C: Dependency maps are a CMDB feature, separate from the change timeline.
distractor_notes.D: Knowledge article lists belong to Knowledge Management.

stem: What does the Change Advisory Board (CAB) workbench enable a CAB manager to do?

options.text: Schedule, plan, and manage CAB meetings
Run CMDB discovery
Resolve incidents on behalf of agents
Author knowledge articles

rationale: The CAB workbench is the CAB manager's command center for scheduling, planning, and managing CAB meetings — agendas, attendees, and the change schedule all in one place.

distractor_notes.B: Discovery is run by ITOM Discovery, not the CAB workbench.
distractor_notes.C: Resolving incidents is an Incident Management activity.
distractor_notes.D: Authoring articles is Knowledge Management.

stem: A CAB definition in ServiceNow is most similar to which of the following?

options.text: A recurring meeting invitation that determines the attributes of all CAB meetings generated from it
A single change request record
A CMDB identification rule
An incident SLA definition

rationale: Think of a CAB definition as a recurring meeting invite: it sets the attributes that every CAB meeting spun up from that definition will inherit. Creating one requires the CAB manager role.

distractor_notes.B: A CAB definition generates meetings; it isn't a single change record.
distractor_notes.C: Identification rules are CMDB configuration.
distractor_notes.D: SLA definitions set response/resolution targets, unrelated to CAB meetings.

stem: What is the role of change approval policies?

options.text: They use approval definitions to generate approvals according to your business requirements
They detect scheduling conflicts between changes
They calculate the CMDB health score
They auto-close resolved incidents

rationale: Change approval policies hold approval definitions that generate the right approvals for a change based on your business rules — codifying who must sign off and when.

distractor_notes.B: Detecting scheduling clashes is conflict detection's job.
distractor_notes.C: CMDB health is a Data Foundations metric.
distractor_notes.D: Auto-closing incidents is an Incident Management behavior.

stem: What does the Change models feature let change managers do?

options.text: Tailor change activities and flows for specific use cases with fit-for-purpose state models
Restore failed services without approvals
Identify the root cause of recurring incidents
Generate the CMDB baseline

rationale: Change models let managers shape fit-for-purpose change processes — custom activities and flows for particular use cases — extending the standard ITIL types rather than forcing one rigid flow.

distractor_notes.B: Restoring failed services without approvals is closer to an emergency-change action, not what change models are.
distractor_notes.C: Root cause is Problem Management.
distractor_notes.D: Generating the CMDB baseline is a Data Foundations activity.

stem: Which of the following can you define using Change models?

options.text: Fit-for-purpose state models
State transitions
State transition conditions
CMDB identification rules
The incident priority matrix

rationale: Change models let you define fit-for-purpose state models, the transitions between those states, and the conditions that gate each transition. Identification rules and the incident priority matrix belong to other areas entirely.

distractor_notes.D: Identification rules are CMDB / Data Foundations configuration, not part of change models.
distractor_notes.E: The incident priority matrix is defined by priority lookup rules in Incident Management.

stem: Why would you create a change model?

options.text: To configure the states and transitions that match your organization's change processes
To delete all standard changes
To assign incidents to groups
To run discovery on a CI

rationale: Creating a change model is how you bake your organization's specific change process into states and transitions, so changes of that type follow the flow you actually use.

distractor_notes.B: Creating a model doesn't delete standard changes.
distractor_notes.C: Incident assignment is an Incident Management activity.
distractor_notes.D: Running discovery is an ITOM activity.

stem: What do you do when you configure change model states?

options.text: Define the states for a change model and the transitions between them
Set the CMDB class hierarchy
Configure the global search sources
Define incident on-hold reasons

rationale: Configuring change model states is where you lay out the states a change passes through and how it moves between them — the skeleton of the model's flow.

distractor_notes.B: The CMDB class hierarchy is Data Foundations configuration.
distractor_notes.C: Global search sources are a platform UI setting.
distractor_notes.D: On-hold reasons belong to the incident state model.

stem: Why would you attach a process to a change model's states?

options.text: To enable state transitions based on defined conditions
To delete the change model
To grant all users the admin role
To recalculate CMDB health

rationale: Attaching a process with defined conditions to model states is what actually drives the transitions — it lets the change move from one state to the next when the conditions are met.

distractor_notes.B: Attaching a process configures transitions; it doesn't delete the model.
distractor_notes.C: It doesn't grant roles.
distractor_notes.D: CMDB health is unrelated to change model transitions.

references.title: Attach a process for Change model states

stem: What is the purpose of the Change Models properties?

options.text: To enable access to the Change models capabilities when creating a change request
To define the company's holiday schedule
To configure incident SLAs
To set up the MID Server

rationale: The Change Models properties switch on access to the change models capabilities so they're available when you create a change request.

distractor_notes.B: Holiday schedules are a platform schedule setting, not change model properties.
distractor_notes.C: Incident SLAs are configured in SLA definitions.
distractor_notes.D: MID Server setup is discovery infrastructure.

stem: What do Change Management change flows provide?

options.text: A library of reusable actions and end-to-end implementations of the base-system change models
A list of all closed incidents
The CMDB identification engine
The knowledge base taxonomy

rationale: Change flows are the prebuilt plumbing: a library of reusable actions plus full end-to-end implementations of the base change models you can use or adapt.

distractor_notes.B: Closed incident lists are an Incident Management view.
distractor_notes.C: The identification engine (IRE) is a CMDB / Data Foundations component.
distractor_notes.D: Knowledge taxonomy is Knowledge Management.

stem: Starting with the Yokohama release, what is the relationship between the new base-system change flows and the existing change workflows?

options.text: The new base-system flows replace the existing workflows, though you can still create or use custom workflows
Flows are forbidden and only workflows may be used
Workflows are deleted automatically on upgrade
Flows only work for incidents, not changes

rationale: From Yokohama onward, base-system flows replace the old workflows for Change Management. You're not forced off custom workflows, but new requirements should be built as flows.

distractor_notes.B: Flows are the recommended direction, not forbidden.
distractor_notes.C: Existing workflows aren't auto-deleted; you can continue using them.
distractor_notes.D: These flows are specifically for Change Management.

stem: Which tool is used to create, operate, and troubleshoot Change Management flows?

options.text: Workflow Studio
The CMDB Workspace
The Service Catalog designer
The Knowledge editor

rationale: Flows are built and managed in Workflow Studio, the single interface that offers natural-language descriptions, runtime information, and consolidated configuration.

distractor_notes.B: The CMDB Workspace is for Data Foundations work.
distractor_notes.C: The catalog designer builds request items.
distractor_notes.D: The Knowledge editor authors articles.

stem: Under which Workflow Studio spoke are the Change Management flow actions available?

options.text: The ITSM spoke
The Discovery spoke
The HR spoke
The Integration Hub spoke for email

rationale: Change Management's Workflow Studio actions live under the ITSM spoke, where they serve as building blocks for handling change models and types.

distractor_notes.B: The Discovery spoke is for ITOM discovery actions.
distractor_notes.C: The HR spoke is for HR Service Delivery.
distractor_notes.D: Email is a generic IntegrationHub action, not where the change actions live.

stem: Adding a new change request type to your change process typically involves managing which artifacts?

options.text: Script includes and workflows
CMDB identification rules
Service Graph Connectors
Knowledge categories

rationale: Standing up a new change type isn't just a label — it involves managing the supporting script includes and workflows that drive that type's behavior.

distractor_notes.B: Identification rules are CMDB configuration.
distractor_notes.C: Service Graph Connectors are ingestion tooling.
distractor_notes.D: Knowledge categories belong to Knowledge Management.

references.title: Add a new change request type

stem: Using the CAB workbench, what can a CAB manager do?

options.text: View and manage the details of a CAB meeting and its agenda items
Resolve incidents for the service desk
Edit the CMDB schema
Author and publish knowledge articles

rationale: The CAB workbench gives the CAB manager control over the meeting and its agenda items — viewing and managing the details that make the meeting run.

distractor_notes.B: Resolving incidents is Incident Management.
distractor_notes.C: Editing the CMDB schema is Data Foundations.
distractor_notes.D: Authoring articles is Knowledge Management.

references.title: CAB meeting management using the CAB workbench

stem: As an itil user attending a CAB meeting through the CAB workbench, what can you do if you are also an approver?

options.text: View the agenda items and change schedule, and approve a change request
Delete the CAB definition
Reassign the instance to a new release
Edit other users' roles

rationale: Attendees see the agenda items and the change schedule in the workbench, and if you hold approver rights you can approve a change request right from the meeting.

distractor_notes.B: Deleting CAB definitions is a CAB manager configuration task, not a general attendee action.
distractor_notes.C: Release upgrades are a platform operation.
distractor_notes.D: Editing roles is an admin task unrelated to attending a CAB.

references.title: CAB meeting attendance using the CAB workbench

stem: Besides recurring CAB meetings from a definition, what else can you create when your requirements call for it?

options.text: An individual, single CAB meeting occurrence
A duplicate of the entire CMDB
A new incident state model
A standard change without a record

rationale: When a one-off is needed, you can create a single CAB meeting occurrence rather than relying solely on the recurring meetings generated by a CAB definition.

distractor_notes.B: Duplicating the CMDB is unrelated and not a thing you do for a CAB.
distractor_notes.C: Incident state models are Incident Management configuration.
distractor_notes.D: Standard changes still create records.

references.title: Create a single CAB meeting occurrence

stem: Why would you add agenda items to a CAB meeting?

options.text: To customize the agenda and make the meeting more effective
To delete change requests in bulk
To recalculate change risk scores
To run conflict detection

rationale: Adding agenda items lets you tailor what the CAB covers, keeping the meeting focused and effective rather than generic.

distractor_notes.B: Agenda items don't bulk-delete changes.
distractor_notes.C: Risk scores come from the risk lookup, not agenda items.
distractor_notes.D: Conflict detection is a separate scheduling function.

references.title: Add new CAB meeting agenda items

stem: What is the purpose of the change approval policy decision builder?

options.text: To define the approvals that should be generated for a change
To build CMDB dependency maps
To author knowledge articles
To schedule maintenance windows

rationale: The decision builder is where you express, via conditions, which approvals a change should generate — codifying your approval logic into a policy.

distractor_notes.B: Dependency maps are a CMDB visualization.
distractor_notes.C: Article authoring is Knowledge Management.
distractor_notes.D: Maintenance windows are scheduled separately, not in the approval decision builder.

references.title: Create a Change approval policy using decision builder

stem: What do Decision records contain in the context of change approval policies?

options.text: The conditions used to determine the change approval action
The list of affected CIs
The change's planned start and end dates
The caller's contact details

rationale: A Decision record holds the conditions that decide the approval action — built with the condition builder so the policy applies the right approval definition when those conditions match.

distractor_notes.B: Affected CIs are captured on the change, not in the decision record's conditions.
distractor_notes.C: Planned dates drive scheduling/conflict detection, not the approval decision conditions.
distractor_notes.D: Caller contact details aren't what a decision record stores.

stem: What does the Change Approval Policy workflow activity do?

options.text: Creates user and group approvals according to a change approval policy record
Detects scheduling conflicts
Closes related incidents
Runs CMDB reconciliation

rationale: The Change Approval Policy workflow activity generates the user and group approvals dictated by a change approval policy record — and you can use multiple activities referencing the same or different policies.

distractor_notes.B: Conflict detection is a separate scheduling feature.
distractor_notes.C: Closing incidents is Incident Management.
distractor_notes.D: Reconciliation is a CMDB / IRE function.

stem: Which records can you copy details from when creating a new change request via the copy feature?

options.text: An active or canceled change request
Only a closed incident
Only a problem record
Only a knowledge article

rationale: The copy feature lets you start a new change from the details of an active or canceled change request — handy for reusing the setup of a similar prior change.

distractor_notes.B: You copy from change requests, not from incidents.
distractor_notes.C: Problems aren't the source for copying a change.
distractor_notes.D: Knowledge articles aren't change records to copy from.

stem: How is the ability to copy a change request record controlled?

options.text: Through system properties
By the caller's role only
By the CMDB health score
By the incident auto-close job

rationale: Whether copying a change is available is governed by system properties, so admins can turn the capability on or off for their instance.

distractor_notes.B: It's controlled by configuration properties, not solely the caller's role.
distractor_notes.C: CMDB health doesn't gate the copy feature.

Resolve incidents in bulk

Only the Knowledge base

stem: With the Change Management integration with ITOM Discovery/Visibility, what can happen for a CI with an IP address that is part of a change?

The CI is deleted from the CMDB
The change is auto-rejected
The caller is granted admin rights

The projected software licensing cost of the change
The root cause of related incidents
The caller's satisfaction score

stem: A change proposes adding CPU cores to a server running software licensed per processor. Which integration surfaces the cost impact, and where is it shown on the change?

stem: How do maintenance schedules assigned to configuration items help with change scheduling?

options.text: Assigning maintenance schedules to CIs lets conflict detection determine conflicts in a change schedule when those CIs are added to a change
They automatically approve the change

stem: During an emergency change, an unplanned configuration item change activity occurs. What does ServiceNow do in response?

options.text: An unauthorized change request is created and sent for approvals
The emergency change is automatically closed as successful
The CI is deleted from the CMDB
All related incidents are reopened

rationale: Emergencies move fast, so unplanned CI activity can slip in. ServiceNow catches it by creating an unauthorized change request and routing it for approvals, keeping accountability even under pressure.

distractor_notes.B: Unplanned activity doesn't auto-close the emergency change as successful.
distractor_notes.C: The CI isn't deleted; the unplanned activity is captured for approval.
distractor_notes.D: Related incidents aren't reopened by this.
